Hardening principles
What is the core aim of system hardening?
Reducing attack surface while keeping required functions
Installing as many security products as possible
Making systems impossible for administrators to change
Disabling logging to improve system performance
Hardening removes unnecessary services, accounts and settings and strengthens what remains, without breaking business needs.
m
Baselines
What is a security baseline?
A documented set of required configuration settings
The first backup taken after a system is installed
The minimum hardware needed to run the operating system
A list of every user allowed to log on to a system
Baselines define agreed settings so systems can be configured and audited consistently.
m
Authoritative sources
Which source publishes widely used consensus hardening benchmarks?
The Center for Internet Security (CIS)
The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority
The World Wide Web Consortium
The IEEE 802 standards committee
CIS Benchmarks are consensus-based configuration guides; vendors and agencies also publish baselines.
d
Benchmark levels
Why might an organisation start with CIS Level 1 rather than Level 2?
Level 1 settings are lower-impact and less likely to break functions
Level 1 settings are newer and include features Level 2 lacks
Level 2 is available only for Linux systems, not for Windows
Level 1 removes the need for any further patching activity
Level 1 is a practical baseline; Level 2 adds defence-in-depth settings with more operational impact.
d
Applying safely
Why apply a new baseline to a test group before production?
To find settings that break applications before wide rollout
Because baselines can be legally applied only to test systems
To reduce licence costs for the baseline tools
Because production systems cannot receive Group Policy
Staged rollout with rollback plans prevents outages caused by strict settings.
m
Rollback
What should exist before a hardening change is applied to a production server?
A tested rollback plan, such as a snapshot or backup
A list of every user's personal passwords
A second administrator logged on at the console
A copy of the baseline printed on paper
If a setting breaks a service, a rollback path limits downtime.
d
Common pitfalls
An administrator disables an 'unused' service across all servers and a payroll job fails. Which practice was missing?
Dependency analysis and staged testing
Stronger passwords for the payroll account
More frequent backups of the payroll database
Faster disks on the affected servers
Hardening must confirm what depends on a component before removing it.
m
Linux updates
Why are unattended security updates often enabled on Linux servers?
They apply security fixes promptly without waiting for manual action
They upgrade the distribution to the next major release each night
They remove the need to reboot after kernel updates
They prevent any package from being installed manually
Automatic security updates shorten exposure windows. Kernel updates may still need a planned reboot.
d
SSH hardening
Which pair of sshd settings most reduces password-guessing risk?
PasswordAuthentication no with key-based authentication
Port 2222 with PermitEmptyPasswords yes
X11Forwarding yes with UseDNS no
MaxSessions 100 with LoginGraceTime 0
Disabling password logins and requiring keys removes the target of brute-force attacks. Changing the port only reduces noise.
m
Accounts
Which Linux hardening step applies to accounts?
Removing or locking unused accounts
Giving every account the same password
Setting every shell to /bin/bash
Adding all users to the sudo group
Unused accounts are an unnecessary attack surface; lock or remove them.
d
Mount options
What does mounting /tmp with noexec achieve?
Programs cannot be executed directly from /tmp
Files in /tmp are deleted as soon as they are closed
Only root can create files in /tmp after mounting
The /tmp directory is hidden from directory listings
noexec blocks direct execution of staged binaries; it is a useful but bypassable layer.
d
Kernel parameters
What does setting net.ipv4.ip_forward=0 ensure on a server that is not a router?
The server does not route packets between interfaces
The server stops responding to all incoming pings
The server blocks every outbound connection
The server uses IPv6 for all traffic instead
Hosts that are not routers should not forward traffic; sysctl settings like this reduce misuse.
m
MAC and logging
Why keep SELinux or AppArmor in enforcing mode rather than disabling it?
It confines services so a compromise is limited
It speeds up file access on busy servers
It is required for SSH to accept connections
It removes the need for file permissions
Mandatory access control limits what a compromised process can reach.
m
Windows baselines
How are Windows security baselines typically applied across an organisation?
Through Group Policy or Intune
By editing each user's NTUSER.DAT
By reinstalling Windows each month
Through the Windows Store application
Microsoft publishes baselines that can be imported into GPOs or Intune profiles.
d
BitLocker
What does BitLocker protect against?
Data being read from a lost or stolen powered-off device
Malware running while the user is logged on
Phishing emails reaching the user's inbox
Weak passwords on domain user accounts
Full-disk encryption protects data at rest. It does not stop attacks on a running, unlocked system.
d
Credential Guard
What does Credential Guard use to protect credentials?
Virtualisation-based security to isolate secrets from the OS
A second hard disk that stores passwords offline
A cloud service that keeps passwords off the device
A browser extension that encrypts saved passwords
VBS isolates LSA secrets so that even admin-level malware cannot read them directly from LSASS memory.
m
ASR rules
What are Attack Surface Reduction rules in Microsoft Defender?
Rules that block risky behaviours such as Office spawning child processes
Firewall rules that block all inbound traffic from the internet
Password rules that require longer passphrases
Backup rules that copy files to the cloud daily
ASR rules target common malware behaviours; they should be tested in audit mode first.
m
Host firewalls
What default policy should a host firewall use for inbound connections?
Deny by default, allowing only required services
Allow by default, blocking only known bad addresses
Allow everything from the local subnet and deny the rest
Disable inbound filtering when an EDR is installed
Default deny with explicit allows limits exposure to necessary services.
d
Stateful firewalls
Why does a stateful host firewall not need a rule allowing replies to outbound connections?
It tracks connections and allows related return traffic automatically
Replies use a separate network card that is not filtered
Outbound connections never receive any reply packets
The firewall disables itself while a connection is open
Connection tracking lets return traffic for established connections through.
m
EDR
What does an EDR product add beyond traditional antivirus?
Behavioural telemetry and response actions across endpoints
A replacement for the operating system's file system
A guarantee that no malware can ever run
Automatic patching of every installed application
EDR records endpoint activity, detects suspicious behaviour and lets responders isolate hosts.
d
Default deny on endpoints
What does application allow-listing (for example WDAC) do?
Lets only approved software run
Blocks only software on a known-malware list
Scans every program once a week
Lets users approve their own software
Allow-listing denies everything not approved, which stops much unknown malware but needs careful management.
m
Automated auditing
What does Lynis do on a Linux system?
Audits configuration and suggests hardening improvements
Encrypts the root file system during installation
Replaces systemd as the init system
Blocks network traffic based on reputation
Lynis scans settings and reports warnings, suggestions and a hardening index.
d
Interpreting scores
A hardening index rises from 62 to 78 after changes. What is the right interpretation?
More checks pass, but the score does not prove the system is secure
The system is now immune to the attacks that Lynis tests for
The system is 78% less likely to be attacked than before
The score shows every vulnerability has been patched
Scores measure checklist coverage. Risk depends on context, exposure and the findings that remain.
d
Audit evidence
Why record before-and-after audit results when hardening a system?
They show what changed and support review and rollback decisions
They are required for the operating system licence to remain valid
They replace the need for change management approval
They let attackers see which settings were changed
Evidence of change makes hardening reviewable and supports compliance and troubleshooting.
m
Common misconfigurations
Which item appears in the NSA/CISA top-ten list of cybersecurity misconfigurations?
Default configurations of software and applications
Use of solid-state drives instead of hard disks
Running servers in more than one data centre
Using IPv6 alongside IPv4 on internal networks
The 2023 advisory lists default configurations, weak MFA, poor patching and other common weaknesses.
d
Defence in depth
Why combine a host firewall, EDR, hardening and patching instead of relying on one?
Each layer covers gaps the others miss
Each product cancels out the others' licensing costs
Only combined products can write event logs
Regulators forbid using any single control
No control is perfect; layered defences reduce the chance one failure leads to compromise.
